ai-at-work.title: Dell sharpens data protection strategy as AI reshapes cyber resilience
ai-at-work.excerpt: After Dell Technologies Inc. saw an 88% jump in revenue reported last week, it’s safe to say the hardware and data management company is on a roll. Although the hype is primarily around Dell’s artific
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Dell just posted an 88% revenue jump and is doubling down on data protection because they know AI adoption brings bigger security headaches. For digital workplace teams, this matters because your AI tools are only as trustworthy as the data infrastructure protecting them, and vendor strategy shifts usually precede product announcements worth paying attention to. Honestly, it's refreshing when a hardware vendor actually talks about security instead of just slapping "AI-powered" on everything and calling it innovation.

ai-at-work.dwp_take: IBM is doubling down on enterprise AI by leveraging its mainframe hardware, hybrid cloud infrastructure, and governance capabilities to position itself as foundational AI infrastructure. This matters because digital workplace leaders are scrambling to understand how AI actually gets deployed at scale, and knowing which vendors have the plumbing to support it beats chasing shiny demos. ai-at-work.title: Augment Code launches Cosmos to bring agentic AI software development to teams
ai-at-work.excerpt: Augment Code Computing Inc., an artificial intelligence agent platform provider, Thursday announced the launch of Cosmos, a service it says is designed to push beyond the era of individual AI coding a
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Augment Code just launched Cosmos, a platform that moves AI coding assistance from individual tools to coordinated team-based systems for engineering groups. This matters because digital workplace leaders are watching how AI collaboration tools reshape how distributed teams actually build software together, not just how individuals work faster. Here's the thing though: we've heard "revolutionary team coordination" promises before, and what usually happens is people keep using whatever's easiest on their laptop while the shiny platform collects dust in the procurement folder.

ai-at-work.title: OpenGov and Snowflake build a knowledge graph to unify government data and AI
ai-at-work.excerpt: Government software is facing the same information management crisis as every other enterprise sector, and the knowledge graph is emerging as the architectural answer. Nickhil Tekwani (pictured, secon
ai-at-work.dwp_take: OpenGov and Snowflake are building a knowledge graph to help government agencies connect fragmented data and improve AI capabilities. This matters because government workers are drowning in disconnected systems just like corporate employees, and a unified data layer could actually make their tools useful instead of frustrating. The irony is that government tech usually lags five years behind the private sector, so if they're finally tackling data silos with knowledge graphs, the rest of us should probably pay attention to what actually works.

tools-tech.title: Asana launches AI ‘chief of staff’ to keep projects on track
tools-tech.excerpt: Asana has launched an AI personal assistant that can track various data sources to alerts users when a work project runs into problems and recommends next actions. It’s one of a range of product annou
tools-tech.dwp_take: Asana rolled out an AI assistant that monitors project data across multiple sources and alerts teams when things go sideways, plus recommends next steps. This matters because digital workplace pros are constantly drowning in status updates and context switching, so an AI that actually catches problems before they spiral could save real time and headaches. The real test is whether it'll become another notification your team ignores or if Asana actually built something useful that doesn't sound like a corporate buzzword generator.

digital-culture.title: The efficiency trap
digital-culture.excerpt: When I became a mother, I closed my office door. Not dramatically—no manifesto, no announcement. I just needed to get more work done in less time, and open doors invite conversations that consume minu
digital-culture.dwp_take: A professor traded open-door accessibility for closed-door productivity after becoming a mother, realizing she needed to protect time by limiting informal interactions. This matters because it exposes the real tension in modern workplace design: we've optimized for efficiency at the expense of the spontaneous conversations that actually generate innovation and culture. The irony is brutal, and any workplace that claims to value both collaboration and individual productivity without addressing this trade-off is just paying lip service to both.

digital-culture.title: Summer is the season that breaks working parents
digital-culture.excerpt: Every June, the school year ends, and the framework that kept us afloat all year vanishes. If you’re lucky, your child is in camp. If you’re very lucky, camp goes past 3 p.m. And if you’re really luck
digital-culture.dwp_take: Every June, working parents lose the structural support that school provides, forcing them to scramble for childcare coverage for three months. This matters to digital workplace leaders because summer productivity takes a predictable nosedive, remote work arrangements get tested, and retention risk spikes for parents who can't make the math work. Here's the thing: we've known this problem exists for decades, yet most organizations still treat June like a surprise rather than planning around it with flexible policies that actually acknowledge reality.

digital-culture.title: Behind the rise of the chief productivity officer and what it means for companies and employees
digital-culture.excerpt: Some employers are replacing HR directors with chief productivity officers to better align people, tech and business outcomes.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Some companies are hiring chief productivity officers to replace traditional HR directors, betting this role will better connect people strategy with technology and business results. This matters because it signals a fundamental shift in how organizations value what used to be called "human resources" - now it's about measurable output rather than employee experience. Honestly, if your company needs a new C-suite title to figure out how to connect people with the tools they need to work effectively, you've already got a bigger problem than an org chart can fix.

digital-culture.title: Hiring program in energy tech sector enlists military veterans to fill data center skills gap
digital-culture.excerpt: With an unprecedented surge in demand for skilled technicians, Schneider Electric eyes talent with military experience.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Schneider Electric launched a hiring program targeting military veterans to fill open data center technician roles as demand for skilled workers outpaces supply. This matters because digital workplace infrastructure depends entirely on people who can keep the lights on, and any talent shortage ripples through every organization relying on cloud services and on-prem systems. The real play here is that veterans already know how to work in high-stress, mission-critical environments where failure isn't an option, which frankly beats most corporate training programs by a mile.

The real story here isn't the headlines but the fact that by Monday morning, your CEO will ask about AI and your security team will ask about patches, and you'll get to explain why you can't just pick one.

industry-news.title: Cisco Warns Agentic AI Will Put New Pressure on Enterprise Networks
industry-news.excerpt: Cisco executives said agentic AI could triple network traffic, creating new infrastructure and security demands for enterprises. The post Cisco Warns Agentic AI Will Put New Pressure on Enterprise Net
industry-news.dwp_take: Cisco is warning that agentic AI systems could triple network traffic, which would require enterprises to beef up their infrastructure and security measures. This matters to digital workplace leaders because they're the ones who have to actually manage these networks while supporting users, and suddenly your "business as usual" bandwidth planning becomes a fairy tale. Of course, Cisco warning about network strain is like a car salesman warning you that driving fast uses more gas, but they're not entirely wrong here and it's worth taking seriously.

industry-news.title: Malicious Hugging Face Models Could Trigger Remote Code Execution
industry-news.excerpt: A flaw in Hugging Face Transformers could allow malicious AI models to execute code, exposing credentials and highlighting AI supply chain risks. The post Malicious Hugging Face Models Could Trigger R
industry-news.dwp_take: Hugging Face, a popular AI model repository, has a vulnerability that lets bad actors hide malicious code in AI models, which then executes on your systems when you download and run them. Digital workplace teams increasingly use open source AI models for everything from chatbots to content generation, so this directly impacts your security posture and vendor risk management. Here's the thing: we spent decades teaching people not to run random executables from the internet, and now we're doing exactly that with AI models because they feel safer somehow. They really don't.
